name: Hydrafacial

card.summary: A branded in-clinic cleansing and exfoliating facial that uses suction and serums; popular and low-downtime, with only a small published evidence base.
card.note: Cosmetic maintenance treatment; published studies are few, small and often manufacturer-linked.

quick.overview:
Hydrafacial is a branded, multi-step facial given by aestheticians or clinicians. It cleanses and exfoliates the skin, uses suction to clear pores, and then applies serums. It is a type of hydradermabrasion, which is itself classed as a variant of microdermabrasion.

It is discussed in skincare and appearance communities as a low-downtime option for a temporary glow and smoother texture. Published research is limited to a few small studies, including a 20-person open-label acne study and an imaging study of skin changes.
quick.mechanism: A handheld tip delivers a water-based solution and exfoliating agents to the skin while applying suction, removing dead surface cells and debris, followed by serums. The effect is superficial exfoliation rather than deep remodelling.
quick.risks: General microdermabrasion-type procedures are described as having few side effects, with temporary dryness, sun sensitivity or rare bruising reported. Results are temporary, so sessions are repeated. Costs vary by clinic.

lead: Hydrafacial is a branded facial treatment that combines cleansing, chemical exfoliation, suction-based extraction and serum application using a single handheld device. It is commonly described as a form of hydradermabrasion, which encyclopedias class as a type of microdermabrasion using water-based sprays and a textured tip [3].

It is offered in aesthetic clinics and spas and is discussed online as a maintenance treatment for a short-term glow and smoother skin. Published studies are few: an imaging study using line-field confocal optical coherence tomography examined microscopic skin changes [1], and an open-label trial in mild-to-moderate acne enrolled 20 adults [2].

paras: The treatment is delivered in stages: cleansing and peeling, suction-based extraction, and infusion of serums. The acne study describes a three-step process of this kind [2]. Hydradermabrasion is classed as a type of microdermabrasion, a non-invasive exfoliation that removes the outermost dead cells and is typically repeated every few weeks [3].

A 2024 study used line-field confocal optical coherence tomography, a non-invasive imaging method, to visualise microscopic anatomical changes after hydradermabrasion. Its authors note that clinical studies validating the procedure with objective histological assessment have been scarce [1].
A 12-week multicenter open-label study enrolled 20 adults with mild-to-moderate acne who were to receive six Clarifying Treatments, one every two weeks [2].

Registered trials include a phase 4 study of three treatments on skin quality, hydration and barrier in 27 adults [4], and scalp studies of the Keravive variant in androgenetic alopecia (44 participants) [5] and self-perceived hair thinning (15 participants, not yet recruiting) [6].

Microdermabrasion in general is described as having few side effects, with temporary dryness, sun sensitivity or, rarely, bruising and scratches reported. Crystal-based systems carry additional risks such as eye injury, which do not apply to water-based designs [3].

Hydrafacial appears in skincare discussions as a convenient pre-event or maintenance treatment. Because results are temporary, it is usually discussed alongside, not as a replacement for, daily skincare and medical acne treatment.
